extracted.intended_audience: non-native English-speaking mathematicians writing research papers and referee reports
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and ready-made phrasing for composing mathematical research papers (abstracts, introductions, definitions, theorems, proofs) and referee reports in idiomatic mathematical English, plus a dictionary of common mathematical idioms and grammar pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard sentence openings and conventions for abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We prove that …"; "Let X be a …. We show that ..."; "We extend a result of [Author] to ..."; passive phrasing such as "It is shown that ..." is documented (acceptable but discouraged). Use concise, declarative statements of main results and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional phrases and organization sentences used in introductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Throughout the paper, we assume ..."; "Our main result is the following:"; "The main idea of the proof is to ..."; "We use the following notation ..."; "The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we ..." — guide to signaling assumptions, main results, proof ideas, notation, and paper structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard wording for introducing definitions and terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "A is said to be B if ..."; "We call A a B if ..."; "By A we mean ..."; "A is defined to be ..." — use these formulaic patterns to introduce precise definitions and names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional forms for labeling and stating theorems, propositions, and lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Theorem 1. Let X be ... Then ..."; "Proposition 2. Suppose that ... Under these assumptions, ..."; "Lemma 3. For every ... there exists ..." — follow standard syntactic patterns to make hypotheses and conclusions clear and formally separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical openings, proof-structure phrases, and closings used in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Proof. We argue by induction on n ..."; "Suppose, for contradiction, that ..."; "It suffices to show that ..."; "By the previous lemma, ..."; "This completes the proof." — use these conventional markers to guide logical flow and signal proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard phrasing and content items for referee/reviewer reports on mathematical manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The paper is well-written and presents new results."; "I recommend acceptance with minor revisions."; "The proof of Theorem 2 contains a gap on page X." — model language for clear evaluative comments, recommendations, and pointing out specific problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles (a / the / Ø)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for using definite, indefinite, or zero article in mathematical contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "the" when the object is unique or previously introduced; use "a" when first introduced; use no article (Ø) for plural, mass, or abstract nouns (e.g., "homotopy theory", "compactness arguments"). Examples: "the function f" vs. "a function from X to Y".

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitives vs. -ing forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on choosing infinitive or gerund constructions common in math English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We aim to prove" and "We aim at proving" are both possible; the book documents which is more common in mathematical English. Prefer "It is necessary to show" rather than ungrammatical or uncommon forms such as "It is necessary showing." Consult examples for idiomatic preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on the acceptability and preferred uses of passive constructions in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical English uses passive voice more than literary English and this is not necessarily a fault. Phrases like "It is well known that ..." are acceptable. Nevertheless, use "we" when the agent is the author (authors' actions are often better stated in the active).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice on use and disambiguation of quantifiers in mathematical prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Any" can be ambiguous in math; replace with "every" or "some" as appropriate. "Each" emphasizes the individual element, "every" the collection. Use "all" with plurals and "every" with singular forms (grammar/semantic distinctions matter for clarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for numerals, spelling numbers, and referring to equations and labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out numbers under ten; use digits for numbers ≥ 10. Refer to displayed equations by number like "(3)" rather than "Eq. (3)". Maintain consistent notation and follow typical mathematical conventions for labelling and referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation rules relevant to mathematical sentences and formula explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a comma before "where" in formula explanations; do not put a comma before "that" in restrictive clauses. Ensure comma use in displayed-equation lists matches surrounding English punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenation rules for compound adjectives and common mathematical descriptors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hyphen in "well-known result" (hyphen before noun) but not in "the result is well known" (predicate form). Examples: "real-valued function", "non-trivial example".

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical English Usage: A Dictionary (idiom distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A glossary-style resource that distinguishes common mathematical idioms and advises which to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries distinguish near-synonyms and their appropriate uses, e.g., "follows from" vs. "is implied by", "is true" vs. "holds", "we have" vs. "there is", "given" vs. "fixed" — explains meanings and contexts to help choose the correct phrase.
